Character frequency and duplicate characters in a string, with streams

String.chars() returns an IntStream, so box each value with mapToObj(c -> (char) c). Passing LinkedHashMap::new as the map factory keeps first-occurrence order, which matters for the next question. O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters.
First non-repeating (and first repeating) character with streams

The LinkedHashMap is the key detail: with a plain HashMap, "first" would mean hash order, not string order. The second version relies on a side-effecting lambda, which is fine for a sequential stream but not safe in a parallel one; say so if you use it.
Names per department (groupingBy + mapping), and min and max salary in one pass (teeing)

mapping transforms each element before it reaches the downstream collector, so you get names rather than whole Employee objects. Other useful downstream collectors: filtering, flatMapping, collectingAndThen. teeing feeds every element into two collectors and combines both results, so you avoid streaming the list twice.
anyMatch / allMatch / noneMatch, and takeWhile / dropWhile

All three match operations short-circuit: they stop as soon as the answer is known. takeWhile is not a filter; it stops at the first failing element, so it is most useful on sorted data or infinite streams.
reduce, IntStream ranges, and Stream.iterate (sum, factorial, Fibonacci)

The identity value must be neutral for the operation (0 for sum, 1 for product). Without an identity, reduce returns an Optional because the stream might be empty. Prefer primitive streams (IntStream, LongStream) for numbers: they avoid boxing and give you sum(), average() and range().
Partition primes and non-primes; anagram and palindrome checks with streams
partitioningBy always returns both keys (true and false), even if one list is empty, unlike groupingBy. The prime check is O(√n) per number; the sorted-chars anagram check is O(n log n).
Laziness, peek, and parallel stream pitfalls (what does this print?)

Elements flow one at a time through the whole pipeline ("vertical" processing), and nothing runs until a terminal operation is called. peek is meant for debugging only; it may not run at all if the pipeline can skip it (for example count() on a sized stream). Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool: they help only for large, CPU-bound, easily splittable data (arrays, ranges), and hurt for small lists, I/O work or ordered operations like limit and findFirst.
Split a list into batches of 3 (Java 24 Gatherers, and the pre-24 way)

Batching is a common "process records in chunks of N" task (bulk inserts, API calls with a size limit). subList returns views of the original list, so copy them with new ArrayList<>(...) if the source might change. Gatherers (Stream.gather) were finalized in Java 24; on Java 21 mention them as the newer option and use the index approach.
Stream.toList() vs collect(Collectors.toList()) vs Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()

| .toList() (Java 16+) | Collectors.toList() | Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()
Can you add/remove? | No (throws) | Not guaranteed by the spec; an ArrayList today | No (throws)
Null elements | Allowed | Allowed | NullPointerException
Typing | Shortest | Works on Java 8 | Java 10+
Use when | Default choice for results | You must mutate the list afterwards (better: toCollection(ArrayList::new)) | You want nulls rejected
Rule of thumb: use .toList(); if the caller needs a mutable list, ask for one explicitly with Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new) instead of relying on what Collectors.toList() happens to return.
groupingBy vs partitioningBy vs toMap: which collector?

| groupingBy | partitioningBy | toMap
Key | Any classifier result | Only true / false | Any key function
Value | List by default, or a downstream collector | List by default, or a downstream collector | One value per key
Duplicate keys | Grouped (that is the point) | Grouped | IllegalStateException unless you pass a merge function
Empty groups | Missing from the map | Both keys always present | n/a
Null key | NullPointerException | Not possible | Allowed by HashMap, but a null value throws
Rule of thumb: many values per key → groupingBy; a yes/no split → partitioningBy; exactly one value per key (id → name) → toMap with a merge function if duplicates are possible.
reduce vs collect: what is the difference?

| reduce | collect
Kind | Immutable reduction: combine two values into a new value | Mutable reduction: add into a container
Good for | Sum, max, product, string of a few items | Lists, maps, StringBuilder, statistics
Cost on collections | Creates a new container per element if misused | One container per thread
Parallel rule | Identity and accumulator must be associative and stateless | Supplier gives each thread its own container, combiner merges them
Interview tip: never use reduce with an ArrayList identity and add inside: it mutates a shared identity and breaks in parallel. That job belongs to collect. For numbers, mapToInt(...).sum() is clearer than reduce(0, Integer::sum).
Stream vs plain for-loop: when is each the better choice?

| Stream | for-loop
Reads like | What you want (filter, map, group) | How to do it, step by step
Checked exceptions inside | Awkward (wrap them) | Natural
break / early return, several outputs | Only via short-circuit ops | Easy
Changing local variables | Not allowed (effectively final) | Allowed
Performance | Small overhead; boxing unless you use IntStream | Usually a bit faster on small data
Debugging | Harder stack traces | Simple
Rule of thumb: streams for transform-and-collect pipelines, loops when you need indexes, early exits, checked exceptions or several results at once. Readability is the deciding factor, not speed.
findFirst vs findAny vs anyMatch vs filter().count() > 0

| findFirst | findAny | anyMatch | filter().count() > 0
Returns | Optional (first in encounter order) | Optional (any element) | boolean | boolean
Short-circuits | Yes | Yes | Yes | Not guaranteed
Parallel streams | Has to respect order, slower | Faster, result may differ run to run | Fast | Counts the matches first
Use for | "The first match" | "Any match will do" | "Is there a match?" | Avoid
Rule of thumb: asking a yes/no question → anyMatch. Need the element → findFirst, or findAny on a parallel stream when order does not matter.
